scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4535: HELP!! The IT and CS departments have been CUT OFF
from each other!! From the department head's machine (it_hod) none of the CS
computers (the 192.168.2.x ones) answer any more -- our own department is
fine, it's just CS that's gone. The router that joins the two departments has
obviously dropped one of its sides -- it's still talking to us but it has let
go of CS, one hundred percent!! Please plug the CS side back into the router
and rejoin the departments!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 connects IT (192.168.1.0/24) and CS
  (192.168.2.0/24) and routes between them; it_hod reaches CS hosts (192.168.2.x)
  with 0% loss. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis of an inter-department routing fault that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- IT (192.168.1.x) cannot
reach CS (192.168.2.x) -- is NOT reproducible: router0's IT and CS interfaces
(192.168.1.1 / 192.168.2.1) are up, ripd is running, and it_hod reaches
192.168.2.x with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: inter-department routing is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the IT->CS path,
finds it working, checks router0's interfaces and RIP/connected routes, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a dropped interface or a missing route to
satisfy the ticket is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The helpdesk ticket asserts that IT department hosts cannot reach CS
department hosts (192.168.2.x), and attributes the fault to router0 having
"dropped" its CS-side interface. Direct live inspection of the network
disproves this entirely.

router0's CS-facing interface (eth1, 192.168.2.1/24) is fully UP with the
correct IP address and is carrying traffic. Its IT-facing interface (eth0,
192.168.1.1/24) and WAN interface (eth2, 10.10.0.1/8) are equally healthy.
The FRR RIP daemon on router0 is correctly advertising both 192.168.1.0/24
and 192.168.2.0/24. switch1, which bridges router0.eth1 to the CS LAN
(lan_cs), has both ports in the UP state and its bridge is forwarding
normally.

End-to-end ICMP tests run directly from it_hod (192.168.1.2) to every
tested CS host — cs_hod (192.168.2.2), cs_lab1 (192.168.2.3), cs_lab3
(192.168.2.5), and cs_lab4 (192.168.2.6) — all returned 4/4 packets with
zero loss and sub-2 ms round-trip times, consistent with a single-hop
routed path through router0.

Root cause: there is no network fault; the symptom described in the ticket
does not match the actual state of the lab.

Corrective action: No configuration change is required. The IT-to-CS path
through router0 is intact and working correctly. The helpdesk team should
re-verify the issue from the physical endpoint that originally reported the
outage — the problem may have been transient, self-healed, or was never
present on the network layer.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly confirms router0's IT (eth0) and CS (eth1) interfaces are up and that inter-department routing works (RIP adverts present and ICMP tests show 0% loss).

The agent's log contains concrete observations (successful pings, router interface states, RIP config, switch link states) that directly support the conclusion of no network fault; the inferences follow logically and the key checks needed to rule out the reported routing failure were performed.
